1.Na3.name: Durkin Opening
1.Na3.background: Named after Robert T. Durkin (1923–2014) of New Jersey, who published his analysis of it in 1959. Also called the Sodium Attack, since Na is the chemical symbol for sodium.

1.Na3 e5.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn and frees the f8-bishop at once, since the knight on the rim does nothing about either. Black also gets the threat of ...Bxa3, which would damage White's pawn structure, so White has to spend time on the knight's problems.

1.Na3 g6.strategy: A sound fianchetto that prepares to bring the bishop to g7 and leaves White to show what the knight on a3 is for. It is less direct than occupying the centre with a pawn, so Black gives up some of the early space that White's passive first move offers.

1.Na3 d5.strategy: Occupies the centre and frees the c8-bishop, so Black develops easily while the knight on the rim still looks for a job. The f8-bishop stays shut in for now, so the knight is under no pressure yet, but the game is calm and Black has the more comfortable side of it.

1.Na3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and watches e4 and d5 without committing a pawn, leaving the centre to be decided later. It is sound and flexible, but it gives White time to rescue the knight and does not claim space the way a central pawn does.

1.Na3 e5 2.Nc4.strategy: Brings the knight from the rim to a square where it works: it attacks the e5 pawn at once and heads for the centre, and it can no longer be captured by the dark-squared bishop. White gives up a tempo to repair the first move, but ends up with a normal development and a flexible game.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3.strategy: Opens the c1-bishop but ignores the knight's weakness: Black can take it with the f8-bishop and force White to recapture with the b-pawn. White is left with doubled a-pawns and a broken queenside in return for the bishop pair.

1.Na3 e5 2.b3.strategy: Guards the knight indirectly: if ...Bxa3, the c1-bishop recaptures and the pawns stay intact. It also opens the long diagonal for that bishop. The knight stays on the rim and e5 goes unchallenged, so Black takes the centre for free.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3.strategy: Trades the bishop for the misplaced knight and forces White to recapture with the b-pawn. The cost is the bishop, but White's queenside pawns are doubled and isolated for the whole game, a lasting weakness that Black can aim at.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre with a second pawn and frees the c8-bishop while keeping the threat against the knight in reserve. White still has to spend a move on the knight, and Black builds a broad pawn centre in the meantime.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and eyes e4 while the knight on a3 remains loose. It is sound, but it takes no space in the centre and gives White time to repair the first move, so Black passes up the chance to exploit the knight at once.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3.strategy: The only way to win the piece back. White accepts the doubled a-pawns and in return gets the half-open b-file for the rook, and the bishop pair, so the game is about whether the activity outweighs the structure.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.b3.strategy: Hopes to chase the bishop with the c1-bishop, but Black simply takes on c1 or steps back with check, and White never regains the piece. A knight down for nothing, White has no compensation for it.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.Bg5.strategy: Attacks the queen, but the bishop is unprotected and Black takes it: ...Qxg5. White is then two pieces down and has nothing to show for it.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3 d5.strategy: Claims a full pawn centre and opens the c8-bishop. Black's structure is healthy and White's is not, so Black plays for a calm, favourable game and does not need to hurry to exploit the weakened queenside.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight to its natural square, where it eyes e4 and supports the centre. Black keeps a sound structure against White's broken one and can complete development before White's activity matters.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3 Nc6.strategy: Defends the e5 pawn and brings a piece out, a solid and low-risk choice. It blocks the c-pawn and takes no central space, so Black plays for a quiet edge in structure rather than for the initiative.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3 d5 4.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and holds the d4 square, so Black's centre cannot advance easily. It shuts in the c1-bishop for now, and White accepts a slow, compact game in which the bishop pair and the b-file must make up for the broken pawns.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3 d5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight with an attack on the e5 pawn, which no piece defends yet, so Black has to spend a move on it. White gets the pieces out quickly and tries to make the bishop pair and the half-open b-file count.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3 d5 4.Bb2.strategy: Aims the bishop along the long diagonal at the undefended e5 pawn and makes the pawn centre prove itself at once. The bishop uses the diagonal the pawn recapture opened, but it stands on the b-file, where White wants a rook.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3 d5 4.e3 c5.strategy: Adds a third central pawn, takes the d4 square away from White and grabs space on the queenside, where White is weakest. Black builds a broad centre that cramps White's pieces, and the pawn chain makes it hard for White to open the game.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3 d5 4.e3 Nc6.strategy: Answers the question the position asks: the e5 pawn has no defender, and the knight protects it while it develops. Black keeps a healthy structure and a solid centre and can choose the pawn break later, with White's weaknesses to play against.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3 d5 4.e3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight, supports the centre and keeps the pawn structure flexible. The e5 pawn still has no defender, so Black must answer the first attack on it, but nothing forces a concession yet.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3 d5 4.e3 c5 5.R.name: Durkin Opening: Celadon Variation
1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3 d5 4.e3 c5 5.R.strategy: Puts the rook on the half-open b-file, the one real asset White got for the doubled pawns: it attacks the b7 pawn, which the c8-bishop must keep guarded. White plays for activity against Black's wing, accepting a poor pawn structure for it.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3 d5 4.e3 c5 5.N.strategy: Develops the knight and attacks the e5 pawn, which nothing defends, so Black has to answer it. It brings White's pieces into play without hurrying the rook to the b-file, but the weak pawns remain a long-term handicap.

1.Na3 e5 2.d3 Bxa3 3.bxa3 d5 4.e3 c5 5.B.strategy: Eyes the e5 pawn along the long diagonal, but the bishop stands on the half-open b-file, the one asset White got for its pawns, and so gets in the way of a rook. Black defends the pawn and White has gained little.

1.Na3 e5 2.Nc4 Nc6.strategy: The natural reply: Black defends the attacked pawn with a developing move and keeps a firm hold on the centre. White's knight has reached a good square, so Black develops in the usual way and keeps all of the central pawn structure.

1.Na3 e5 2.Nc4 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn and opens the diagonals of both bishops. It is solid and leaves every piece free to develop, at the price of some central space and a slightly passive set-up.

1.Na3 e5 2.Nc4 Qe7.strategy: Defends e5 with the queen and keeps the pawn centre, but the queen blocks the f8-bishop and the e7 square for the king's knight. It is playable and clumsy: Black has to unravel the pieces before the position works.

1.Na3 e5 2.Nc4 Nc6 3.e4.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn and opens lines for the queen and the f1-bishop. White has repaired the opening with the knight on c4, and the tempo spent on the knight's trip is the price for a normal, open game.

1.Na3 e5 2.Nc4 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the second knight and attacks e5 a second time, so Black must defend it again or push it on. White plays for quick development against the centre, while the e5 pawn can gain space by advancing and cramp the knight.

1.Na3 e5 2.Nc4 Nc6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the f1-bishop and leaves the centre alone. It is a slow, flexible set-up: Black has no trouble holding e5 and gets time to build the centre, so White gives up the initiative it could have taken.

1.Na3 e5 2.Nc4 Nc6 3.e4 f5.name: Durkin Opening: Durkin Gambit
1.Na3 e5 2.Nc4 Nc6 3.e4 f5.strategy: Challenges the e4 pawn at once and tries to take the initiative, but weakens the king: the diagonal to e8 is open. A sharp, unbalanced game results, in which White can choose to open lines and punish the loosened position.

1.Na3 e5 2.Nc4 Nc6 3.e4 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on the e4 pawn, which nothing defends, so White has to protect it. Black keeps a sound centre and develops naturally, with no weakness in the king's position, and leaves White to prove that the knight trip was worth the time.

1.Na3 e5 2.Nc4 Nc6 3.e4 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop, building a compact centre against the e4 pawn. Black declines to take the initiative and relies on solid development, a safe way to meet the gambit's idea.

1.Na3 g6 2.g4.name: Durkin Opening: Chenoboskion Variation
1.Na3 g6 2.g4.strategy: Grabs space on the kingside in the hope of a quick attack, but loosens White's own king and does nothing for the knight on the rim. Black answers by developing and striking in the centre, and the advanced pawn becomes a target rather than a spearhead.

1.Na3 g6 2.e4.strategy: Claims the centre at once and opens lines for the queen and the f1-bishop, the plainest way to make good the time the knight on the rim cost. Black's fianchetto bishop will press on the long diagonal, so White must keep the centre firm and bring the knight back into play soon.

1.Na3 g6 2.c4.strategy: Takes space on the queenside and frees c2, so the knight can go there and support the centre. White builds slowly and flexibly instead of occupying the centre with a pawn, and leaves Black the freer game in the middle.
